newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish NBP not firm on slower 97 zloty devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Polish NBP not firm on slower 97 zloty devaluation.

text.p: The planned slow-down in the annual devaluation rate for the Polish zloty to nine percent in 1997 from 12.7 percent in 1996 is only tentative and may not materialise, deputy central bank president said on Tuesday.

The zloty is presently devalued by one percent per month against a basket of five western currencies, in a mechanism known as the crawling peg, to compensate for inflation which was at 18.5 percent year-on-year in December 1996.

"(In the budget law) the government, with our help, assumed the monthly devaluation rate would fall this year to nine percent from more than 12 percent last year, but that's nothing certain," Witold Kozinski told a news conference.
"The budget law is just a projection, an assumption, which may, but does not have to prove true, and the same applies to the monthly zloty devaluation rate," Kozinski said.

For several weeks the zloty has been under appreciation pressure from foreign investors, some of which cited expectations of an NBP cut of the crawling peg this year as one of the reasons for buying zloty instruments.
If the nine percent annual zloty devaluation target was to be met, the central bank would have to slow the crawling peg to 0.7 percent a month already in February.
